people.name: Ezra
people.description: A priest and scribe skilled in the law of Moses who led a company of exiles from Babylon back to Jerusalem under Persian sanction. By publicly reading and teaching the Torah, he re-centered the restored community on Scripture, a legacy foundational to Jewish identity ever after. Ezra 7:1-5 traces his line through Seraiah and Zadok back to Aaron the chief priest, in an abridged list.
people.dateNotes: Came to Jerusalem in the seventh year of Artaxerxes I (Ezra 7:7-8), 458 BC (457 on autumn-to-autumn reckoning), and read the law in Nehemiah's time (Neh 8; 444 BC). Called son of Seraiah (Ezra 7:1), the high priest killed in 588 BC, meaning descendant. Birth and death estimated.

scripture.context: Ezra 7:1-5 gives his line back to Aaron
Leads the families who went up with him
Stood on the pulpit of wood

people.name: Esther
people.description: A Jewish orphan named Hadassah who became queen of Persia in the citadel of Susa and risked her life to expose Haman's plot to annihilate her people. Her courage is celebrated yearly at Purim; the Ahasuerus of her story is commonly identified with Xerxes I of Persian history. She was Mordecai's cousin, the daughter of his uncle Abihail (Esth 2:7, 15), and was raised by him after her parents died.
people.dateNotes: Became queen in the tenth month of the seventh year of Ahasuerus (Esth 2:16), 479/478 BC if he is Xerxes I; Haman's plot falls in his twelfth year (3:7), 474/473 BC. Birth and death estimated.

people.name: Sanballat
people.description: Governor of Samaria who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.
people.dateNotes: Neh 2:10, 19; 4:1-8; 6:1-14. Confirmed by Elephantine Papyri.

people.name: Tobiah
people.description: Ammonite official who opposed Nehemiah's rebuilding and conspired against him.

people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Post-exilic period.

people.name: Geshem the Arabian
people.description: Arab leader who with Sanballat and Tobiah mocked the rebuilding of Jerusalem's wall, and with Sanballat tried to lure Nehemiah to a meeting at Ono to harm him. Nehemiah 6:6 calls him Gashmu.
people.dateNotes: Estimate. Active in 445 BC (Neh 2:19; 6:1-6). Born about 495 BC; death not recorded.

events.role: Opponent who mocked and plotted against Nehemiah (Neh 2:19; 6:1-6)

people.name: Malachi
people.description: Last of the twelve Minor Prophets, who called the restored community back to faithful worship and marriage and promised that Elijah would come before the day of the Lord (Mal 4:5).
people.dateNotes: Usually dated to the mid-5th century BC, c. 460-430, near the time of Ezra and Nehemiah (compare Mal 2:11 with Neh 13:23-29). Birth and death estimated.

people.name: Rehum the chancellor
people.description: Royal officer of the province beyond the River, based in Samaria. With Shimshai the scribe he wrote to Artaxerxes against the Jews rebuilding Jerusalem, and when the king ordered the work stopped he enforced it.
people.dateNotes: Estimate. The letter was sent to a king named Artaxerxes, taken here as Artaxerxes I (reigned 465-424 BC), before Nehemiah's mission of 445 BC (Ezra 4:8-24). Scholars differ on the exact date of the letter. Death not recorded.

events.role: Had written against the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:8-23)

scripture.context: Writes against Jerusalem and stops the work

people.name: Shimshai the scribe
people.description: Scribe who wrote with Rehum the chancellor to King Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of Jerusalem, and helped stop the work by force.
people.dateNotes: Estimate, as for Rehum: active under Artaxerxes I (Ezra 4:8-24). Death not recorded.

events.role: Had written against the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls (Ezra 4:8-23)

people.name: Eliashib the high priest
people.description: High priest in Nehemiah's day. He and his brother priests rebuilt the Sheep Gate, but he was also allied to Tobiah and gave him a chamber in the Temple courts, which Nehemiah threw out. A grandson married a daughter of Sanballat.
people.dateNotes: Estimate. High priest in 445 BC (Neh 3:1) and still in 433 BC (Neh 13:4-7, 28). Born about 490 BC; death not recorded.

events.role: High priest who rebuilt the Sheep Gate (Neh 3:1)

scripture.context: Allied to Tobiah and gives him a Temple chamber
Rebuilt the Sheep Gate with the priests
Joiakim begat Eliashib; Eliashib begat Joiada
Priest over the chamber of the house of God, allied to Tobiah

people.name: Artaxerxes I
people.description: Persian king, son of Xerxes, who sent Ezra to Jerusalem in his seventh year (Ezra 7) and Nehemiah, his cupbearer, in his twentieth (Neh 2:1-8). He also ordered a halt to the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls after complaints from its neighbours (Ezra 4:7-23).
people.dateNotes: Reigned 465-424 BC by Persian and Greek records. Birth estimated. Some scholars identify Ezra's king as Artaxerxes II (404-358 BC).

people.name: Nehemiah
people.description: Cupbearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes who returned as governor of Judah and rebuilt Jerusalem's shattered walls in fifty-two days despite fierce opposition. His memoirs join practical leadership to constant prayer, and with Ezra he anchored the restored community in covenant obedience. His brother Hanani brought him news of Jerusalem (Neh 1:2).
people.dateNotes: Came to Jerusalem in the 20th year of Artaxerxes I (Neh 2:1), 445/444 BC; returned to the king in his 32nd year, 433/432 BC, and later came back (Neh 13:6-7). Birth and death estimated.

people.name: Joiada, high priest
people.description: High priest, son of Eliashib and father of Jonathan; his son married a daughter of Sanballat (Neh 13:28).
people.dateNotes: Estimate by generation from Eliashib (b. about 490 BC).

scripture.context: Son of Eliashib, father of Jonathan
Levites were recorded in his days

people.name: Hanan, son of Zaccur (Neh 13:13)

people.description: Son of Abiud, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:13. Post-exilic figure.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Not the Eliakim of 2 Kings 18. Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Jonathan (Johanan), high priest
people.description: High priest, son of Joiada and father of Jaddua; called Johanan the son of Eliashib in Nehemiah 12:23, probably as a grandson.
people.dateNotes: Estimate by generation from Joiada. Nehemiah 12:11 and 12:23 may compress the line.

scripture.context: Son of Joiada, father of Jaddua
Called Johanan the son of Eliashib

people.name: Azor
people.description: Son of Eliakim, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:13–14.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Jaddua, high priest
people.description: High priest, son of Jonathan and last of the line named in Nehemiah.
people.dateNotes: Estimate by generation from Jonathan.

scripture.context: Levites were recorded in his days

people.name: Philip II of Macedon
people.description: King of Macedon who made Macedon the leading power of Greece and was assassinated in 336 BC. Father of Alexander the Great. Not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Born 382 BC, died 336 BC. Daniel 8:21 and 11:3 speak of the first king of Greece.

people.name: Olympias
people.description: Queen of Macedon, wife of Philip II and mother of Alexander the Great. Not named in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Standard historical record (not stated in Scripture). Born about 375 BC and killed in 316 BC.

people.name: Alexander the Great
people.description: King of Macedon whose conquest of the Persian empire (334-323 BC) ended Persian rule over Judea and spread Greek language and culture across the east. Daniel's vision of the he-goat whose great horn is the first king of Grecia is traditionally read as pointing to him (Dan 8:5-8, 21; 11:3-4), and 1 Maccabees opens with his conquests (1 Macc 1:1-7).
people.dateNotes: Born July 356 BC, died June 323 BC at Babylon. Reading the Daniel passages as Alexander is the traditional interpretation; scholars differ on the dating of Daniel itself.

people.name: Zadok, son of Azor
people.description: Son of Azor, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:14. Not the priest Zadok of David's time.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Not to be confused with Zadok the priest (2 Sam 8:17). Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Achim
people.description: Son of Zadok, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:14.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Intertestamental period. Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Eliud
people.description: Son of Achim, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:14–15.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Intertestamental period. Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Antiochus IV Epiphanes
people.description: Seleucid king who plundered the temple in Jerusalem, banned Jewish practice, and set up the abomination of desolation on its altar in December 167 BC, provoking the Maccabean revolt (1 Macc 1:10-64; 2 Macc 5-6). Many readers link him to the little horn of Dan 8:9-12 and to Dan 11:21-35, while some traditions also read these passages of a later figure.
people.dateNotes: Reigned 175-164 BC and died late in 164 BC in Persia (1 Macc 6:1-16). Birth estimated.

events.role: Seleucid king who ordered the desecration

people.name: Judas Maccabeus
people.description: Third son of the priest Mattathias, who led the Jewish revolt after his father's death in 166 BC, defeated Seleucid armies, and rededicated the temple in December 165 BC (Ussher; standard dating 164 BC), the event commemorated at Hanukkah (1 Macc 3-4; 2 Macc 8-10; John 10:22). He fell in battle at Elasa in 161 BC (1 Macc 9:5-18; Ussher).
people.dateNotes: Died in year 152 of the Seleucid era (1 Macc 9:3): 161 BC on Ussher (Annals §3528-3532); standard dating 160 BC. Birth estimated. The books of Maccabees are canonical for Catholic and Orthodox Christians and counted among the Apocrypha by Protestants.

people.name: Eleazar, son of Eliud
people.description: Son of Eliud, ancestor of Jesus in Matthew 1:15. Not the priest Eleazar son of Aaron.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy. Not to be confused with Eleazar the priest (Num 20:28). Birth year is an inferred placeholder, evenly spaced between Zerubbabel and Joseph (Matt 1:13-16); Matthew's list probably omits generations, as it does in 1:8 and 1:11.

people.name: Matthan
people.description: Son of Eleazar, grandfather of Joseph of Nazareth in Matthew 1:15.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:15). Birth year is an inferred placeholder spacing the ten generations from Zerubbabel to Joseph evenly; Matthew's list is probably selective.

people.name: Pompey
people.description: Roman general who took Jerusalem in 63 BC, ending Hasmonean independence and bringing Judea under Rome; he entered the Holy of Holies but left the Temple treasury untouched (Josephus, Antiquities 14.4). He was killed in Egypt after his defeat by Julius Caesar.
people.dateNotes: Born 106 BC; killed in Egypt in 48 BC. Not named in Scripture.

people.name: Simeon of Jerusalem
people.description: Devout man in Jerusalem who held the infant Jesus and prophesied. Promised he would see the Messiah.
people.dateNotes: Luke 2:25-35. Luke gives no age, only that he would not die before seeing the Lord's Christ (Luke 2:26); birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Anna
people.description: Elderly prophetess who recognized the infant Jesus at the Temple.
people.dateNotes: Luke 2:36-37: daughter of Phanuel of Asher, seven years married, then 'a widow of about fourscore and four years', which may mean aged 84 or widowed 84 years (about 105). Taking 84 as her age at the presentation (c. 5 BC) gives a birth c. 89 BC; the death year is an estimate.

people.name: Matthat, father of Heli
people.description: Son of Levi, ancestor of Jesus in Luke 3:24. Post-exilic Matthat, grandfather of Joseph.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Late Second Temple period.

people.name: Jacob, son of Matthan
people.description: Son of Matthan, father of Joseph of Nazareth in Matthew 1:15–16. Not the patriarch Jacob.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Matthew's genealogy (Matt 1:15-16). Birth year is an inferred placeholder; Matthew's list is probably selective.

people.name: Herod the Great
people.description: King of Judea who rebuilt the Temple but ordered the massacre of infants in Bethlehem. Father of Archelaus, Herod Antipas and Philip the tetrarch, and grandfather of Herod Agrippa I through Aristobulus IV.
people.dateNotes: Matthew 2:1-19; confirmed by Josephus. Death in 4 BC is well-established.

events.role: Began the rebuilding of the temple

people.name: Caesar Augustus
people.description: First Roman emperor (27 BC-AD 14). Luke says his decree that all the world should be taxed brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1-5). Augustus adopted his stepson Tiberius in AD 4 and named him his successor.
people.dateNotes: Born 23 September 63 BC; died 19 August AD 14. Luke 2:1.

events.role: Octavian, who backed the Senate's decree
His census decree brought Joseph and Mary to Bethlehem (Luke 2:1)

people.name: Zechariah, father of John the Baptist
people.description: Priest who was struck mute for doubting Gabriel's announcement of John the Baptist's birth.
people.dateNotes: Luke 1:5-25, 57-80. Luke says only that he and Elizabeth were 'well stricken in years' (Luke 1:7); birth and death years are estimates. A second-century tradition (the Protoevangelium of James), not in Scripture, tells of his murder in the Temple; the Orthodox Church commemorates him as a martyr.

scripture.context: Priest of the course of Abijah (Luke 1:5)

people.name: Heli
people.description: Named in Luke 3:23 as the father of Joseph, in the line running back through Matthat and Levi to Nathan, a son of David. Matthew 1:16 gives Joseph's father as Jacob instead, and the table keeps Matthew's link as Joseph's father_id and shows Heli's link as a separate parent relationship. Two classic explanations are offered. Africanus held that Heli and Jacob were half-brothers, Heli dying childless so that Jacob fathered Joseph by levirate marriage and Joseph counted as Heli's heir. Others hold that Luke gives Mary's ancestry, making Heli Mary's father and Joseph his son-in-law. Scripture does not say which is right.
people.dateNotes: Known only from Luke's genealogy. Some scholars identify Heli as Mary's father, making Luke's genealogy the natural/maternal line.

people.name: Elizabeth
people.description: Wife of Zechariah; mother of John the Baptist. Relative of Mary. Elizabeth was a daughter of Aaron (Luke 1:5) and Mary's "cousin" (Luke 1:36).
people.dateNotes: Luke 1:5-7, 39-45, 57-60. Birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Tiberius Caesar
people.description: Second Roman emperor (AD 14-37). Luke dates the start of John the Baptist's preaching to his fifteenth year (Luke 3:1), and Jesus was crucified under his prefect Pontius Pilate. Born Tiberius Claudius Nero, he was the stepson of Augustus, who adopted him in AD 4.
people.dateNotes: Born 16 November 42 BC; emperor from 19 August AD 14; died 16 March AD 37. Luke 3:1.

events.role: Emperor in whose fifteenth year John began his ministry (Luke 3:1)

people.name: Aristobulus IV
people.description: Son of Herod the Great and the Hasmonean princess Mariamne, put to death by his father with his brother Alexander. He was the father of Herod Agrippa I and of Herodias, and so grandfather of Agrippa II, Bernice and Drusilla (Josephus). He is not named in Scripture; the link to Acts 12 is through his son.
people.dateNotes: Josephus (Ant. 16.394; Jewish War 1.551): executed at Sebaste, about 7 BC. Birth c. 35 BC is inferred from his mother's marriage to Herod in 37 BC. Not in Scripture.

people.name: Caiaphas
people.description: High priest who presided over Jesus' trial; declared it expedient for one man to die for the people. Annas was his father-in-law (John 18:13).
people.dateNotes: Matt 26:3, 57-68; John 11:49-53; 18:13-28. Ussher, Annals §6278: appointed high priest by Valerius Gratus in AD 26, after Annas's removal; deposed by Vitellius in AD 35 (§6543; Josephus Ant. 18.95 has 36/37). The death year marks the deposition; his death is unrecorded. An ossuary found in 1990 may be his (debated). Birth year is an estimate.

people.name: Joseph of Arimathea
people.description: Rich member of the Sanhedrin who provided his tomb for Jesus' burial.

people.name: Jonas, father of Peter
people.description: Father of Simon Peter. Jesus calls Peter "Simon Bar-jona" (Matt 16:17) and "son of Jona" (John 1:42); in John 21:15-17 the KJV reads "son of Jonas". Some manuscripts of John give the name as John. Peter's brother Andrew is presumed to share this father.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only, about a generation before Peter. Scripture gives no dates for him. Andrew is called Peter's brother (John 1:40) but only Peter is named as Jona's son in the text; Andrew's link rests on that.

scripture.context: Simon, son of Jona (KJV Jonas), lovest thou me?

people.name: Lois
people.description: Timothy's grandmother, in whom Paul says the faith first dwelt before it passed to Timothy's mother Eunice and to Timothy (2 Tim 1:5); Eunice is usually taken to be her daughter.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only. Scripture gives no dates.

people.name: Alphaeus, father of Levi
people.description: Named in Mark 2:14 as the father of Levi, the tax collector whom Jesus called, usually identified with the apostle Matthew (Matt 9:9). The Gospels do not say whether he is the Alphaeus who fathered James the Less (Matt 10:3); some later writers assume so, others do not.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only. Scripture gives no dates for him. Kept separate from the Alphaeus of Matt 10:3 because the text does not identify them.

scripture.context: Father of Levi the tax collector

people.name: Joseph of Nazareth
people.description: Husband of Mary and legal father of Jesus, a carpenter of Nazareth described as a righteous man (Matt 1:19). Matthew 1:16 calls him the son of Jacob, and this table follows Matthew for his father. Luke 3:23 calls him the son of Heli, so the two lists disagree. Two classic explanations are offered. Africanus (3rd century) held that Jacob and Heli were half-brothers by the same mother, and that when Heli died childless Jacob married the widow, so Joseph was Jacob's son by birth and Heli's by levirate law. Other writers, including many later Western and Eastern commentators, read Luke as tracing Mary's line, with Heli as her father and Joseph as his son-in-law. The tradition of the church does not require a choice between them.
people.dateNotes: Matthew 1-2; Luke 2. Disappears from narrative after Jesus' youth.

people.name: Annas
people.description: Former high priest and father-in-law of Caiaphas; influential in Jesus' trial.
people.dateNotes: Luke 3:2; John 18:13-24; Acts 4:6. High priest from AD 6 (Josephus Ant. 18.26, 18.34); removed by Gratus (Ussher, Annals §6268 places the removal in AD 23); five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas held the office afterwards. Ussher still calls him high priest at the trial of Stephen (§6519, AD 33), as Acts 4:6 does. Birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Zebedee
people.description: Galilean fisherman, father of the apostles James and John. His sons left him mending nets in the boat with his hired servants to follow Jesus.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only, about a generation before his sons. Scripture gives no dates for him, and he does not appear after the calling of his sons.

scripture.context: Mending nets with his sons when Jesus calls them

people.name: Alphaeus, father of James the apostle
people.description: Father of the apostle James son of Alphaeus (Matt 10:3), traditionally identified with James the Less (Mark 15:40). Mark 2:14 calls Levi (Matthew) "the son of Alpheus" too. Whether this is the same Alphaeus, which would make Matthew and James brothers, is not stated in the Gospels; the two are kept as separate rows here.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only. Scripture gives no dates for him.

people.name: Clopas
people.description: Husband of the Mary who stood by the cross (John 19:25). Tradition links him with the Cleopas of Luke 24:18; Scripture does not say so.
people.dateNotes: Estimate: husband of the Mary who stood by the cross in AD 33 (John 19:25).

scripture.context: Husband of Mary who stood by the cross

people.name: Archelaus
people.description: Son of Herod the Great who ruled Judea, Samaria and Idumea as ethnarch after his father's death. When Joseph heard that Archelaus reigned in Judea in his father's place, he was afraid to go there and turned aside to Galilee (Matt 2:22). Augustus removed him in AD 6 after complaints from his subjects.
people.dateNotes: Josephus (Ant. 17.188; Jewish War 2.111): born c. 23 BC, ethnarch 4 BC to AD 6, banished beyond the Alps (Ussher, Annals §6174, AD 6). The year of his death is uncertain, so none is given.

scripture.context: Joseph fears Archelaus and goes to Galilee

people.name: Philip the Tetrarch
people.description: Son of Herod the Great, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1). He rebuilt Caesarea Philippi and Bethsaida, and according to Josephus married Salome, the daughter of Herodias. He should not be confused with the Philip whom Mark 6:17 calls Herodias's first husband; Josephus names that man as another son of Herod the Great.
people.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6079, §6529: tetrarch from 4 BC (Herod's will); died AD 34 at Julias, in the twentieth year of Tiberius, after governing thirty-seven years (Josephus Ant. 18.106-108). Birth c. 22 BC is inferred from his father's marriage to Cleopatra of Jerusalem.

events.role: Tetrarch named in Luke 3:1 as ruling at the time

people.name: Mary, mother of Jesus
people.description: The young woman of Nazareth chosen to bear Jesus, whose obedient response to the angel's announcement made her the most honored woman in Scripture. Her Magnificat echoes Hannah's song, and she appears from Bethlehem to the cross and among the praying disciples before Pentecost. Luke calls Elisabeth her "cousin" (Luke 1:36), a relative of unspecified degree; the two are not sisters.
people.dateNotes: Birth and death years are estimates. Scripture last mentions her at Acts 1:14. Catholic and Orthodox Christians hold her Assumption or Dormition; Protestants generally hold that Scripture is silent on the end of her life. Tradition places her later life at Jerusalem or Ephesus.

people.name: Nicodemus
people.description: Pharisee who came to Jesus at night; helped bury Jesus.
people.dateNotes: John 3:1-21; 7:50-52; 19:39. Birth c. 20 BC and death c. AD 63 are estimates only: Scripture records neither and no early tradition dates his death.

people.name: Herod Antipas
people.description: Son of Herod the Great; executed John the Baptist and mocked Jesus during his trial.
people.dateNotes: Matt 14:1-12; Mark 6:14-29; Luke 3:1; 13:31-32; 23:6-12. Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea from 4 BC (Ussher, Annals §6079); banished in AD 39 (Ussher, Annals, under 39 AD, citing Josephus Ant. 18.240-255). His birth (c. 20 BC) is inferred and the year of his death is unknown.

events.role: Tetrarch who imprisoned and killed John

people.name: Zacchaeus
people.description: Chief tax collector in Jericho who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus; converted.

events.role: Chief tax collector who received Jesus

people.name: Jairus
people.description: Synagogue ruler whose 12-year-old daughter Jesus raised from the dead.
people.dateNotes: Mark 5:22-43; Luke 8:41-56. Synagogue ruler in Galilee. Daughter raised by Jesus c. AD 31. Birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Mother of James and John
people.description: Wife of Zebedee and mother of the apostles James and John. She asked Jesus that her two sons might sit at his right and left in his kingdom (Matt 20:20-21) and stood among the women at the crucifixion (Matt 27:56). Scripture does not give her name. Mark 15:40 lists a Salome in the same group of women, and many readers identify the two; that is an inference, and some traditions identify her differently. She is not Salome the daughter of Herodias.
people.dateNotes: Estimate only, about a generation before her sons. The identification with Salome (Mark 15:40) is a common inference, not stated in Scripture; compare Matt 27:56 with Mark 15:40.

scripture.context: Asks Jesus for places for her sons
Among the women at the crucifixion
Salome, listed among the women, is commonly identified with her

people.name: Simon the leper
people.description: Host at Bethany of the meal where a woman anointed Jesus (Matthew 26:6; Mark 14:3).
people.dateNotes: Estimate: an adult householder at Bethany in the week of the passion, AD 33 (Matt 26:6; Mark 14:3).

scripture.context: In whose house Jesus was anointed
In whose house Jesus was anointed

people.name: Simon the Pharisee
people.description: A Pharisee who invited Jesus to eat and was told of the two debtors (Luke 7:36-47). Scripture does not equate him with Simon the leper.
people.dateNotes: Estimate: a Pharisee who hosted Jesus in Galilee, about AD 31 (Luke 7:36-50).

scripture.context: Host who invited Jesus to dinner

people.name: Herodias
people.description: Wife of Herod Antipas; orchestrated John the Baptist's execution through her daughter. Her father was Aristobulus IV (Josephus), so she was the sister of Herod Agrippa I and Antipas's niece. Her first husband was another son of Herod the Great (Mark 6:17 calls him Philip; Josephus calls him Herod).

events.role: Wife of Antipas who demanded John's death

people.name: Martha
people.description: Sister of Lazarus and Mary; known for her hospitality and service.
people.dateNotes: Luke 10:38-42; John 11; 12:2. Birth and death years are estimates. Later tradition (Provence) is legendary; Scripture is silent.

people.name: Pontius Pilate
people.description: Roman governor of Judea who authorized the crucifixion of Jesus.
people.dateNotes: Prefect of Judea from AD 26 (Ussher, Annals §6279; Luke 3:1); ordered to Rome by Vitellius in AD 36 (§6564); Ussher, citing Eusebius and Jerome, has him take his own life under Caligula in AD 39 (§6609), a late tradition. Birth year is conjecture.

people.name: Simon of Cyrene
people.description: Man from Cyrene compelled to carry Jesus' cross.
people.dateNotes: Matt 27:32; Mark 15:21; Luke 23:26.

people.name: Mary of Bethany
people.description: Sister of Martha and Lazarus; sat at Jesus' feet; anointed him with expensive perfume.
people.dateNotes: Luke 10:38-42; John 11:1-2; 12:1-8. Birth and death years are estimates. She is distinct from Mary Magdalene; the Western identification of the two (and of the sinful woman of Luke 7) goes back to Gregory the Great (AD 591), was never held in the East, and was dropped from the Roman calendar in 1969.

people.name: Gamaliel
people.description: Respected Pharisee and teacher of Paul; counseled moderation toward the apostles.
people.dateNotes: Acts 5:34-39; 22:3. His counsel falls in AD 33 (Ussher, Annals §6516). Birth and death years are estimates; Scripture gives neither.

events.role: Pharisee and teacher of the law who counselled restraint

people.name: Herod Agrippa I
people.description: Grandson of Herod the Great; executed James son of Zebedee and imprisoned Peter. Struck dead by God. Son of Aristobulus IV, a son of Herod the Great, so grandson of Herod the Great; father of Agrippa II, Bernice and Drusilla, and brother of Herodias (Josephus).
people.dateNotes: Acts 12:1-23. Josephus says he died in AD 44 aged 54 (Ant. 19.343-352), so born c. 11/10 BC.

people.name: Claudius
people.description: Fourth Roman emperor (AD 41-54). Acts dates the famine foretold by Agabus to his reign (Acts 11:28) and says his expulsion of the Jews from Rome brought Aquila and Priscilla to Corinth (Acts 18:2).
people.dateNotes: Born 1 August 10 BC; died 13 October AD 54. The expulsion of the Jews: Ussher (Annals 6792) places it just before Paul reached Corinth, AD 54; Orosius gives AD 49, the usual modern date (compare Suetonius, Claudius 25).

events.role: Emperor in whose reign the famine came

scripture.context: Famine in the days of Claudius

people.name: John of the high priest's family
people.description: Named with Annas, Caiaphas and Alexander among the high priest's kindred at Peter and John's hearing (Acts 4:6).
people.dateNotes: Estimate: of the high priest's family at the council that questioned Peter and John, AD 33 (Acts 4:6).

scripture.context: Of the kindred of the high priest

people.name: Alexander of the high priest's family
people.description: Named with Annas, Caiaphas and John among the high priest's kindred at Peter and John's hearing (Acts 4:6).
people.dateNotes: Estimate: of the high priest's family at the council that questioned Peter and John, AD 33 (Acts 4:6).

scripture.context: Of the kindred of the high priest

people.name: Susanna
people.description: One of the women healed by Jesus who supported him and his disciples from their means (Luke 8:2-3).
people.dateNotes: Estimate: one of the women who ministered to Jesus in Galilee, about AD 31 (Luke 8:3).

scripture.context: Among the women who ministered to Jesus

people.name: Jesus
people.description: The central figure of the Christian faith, proclaimed as Messiah and Son of God, whose teaching, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, and resurrection stand at the heart of the gospel. The Pilate stone from Caesarea and the Caiaphas ossuary attest the very officials named at his trial.
people.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6057: born 5 BC (before Herod's death, Matt 2:1, 19); crucified Friday 3 April AD 33 (§6474-6477). Baptised about thirty (Luke 3:23) in AD 27 (§6288). Many modern scholars place the birth 6-4 BC; AD 30 is the main alternative for the crucifixion.

events.role: Heard of John's death and withdrew
Called Zacchaeus down and stayed at his house

people.name: John the Baptist
people.description: A wilderness prophet who called Israel to repentance and baptism in the Jordan and pointed to Jesus as the coming one. Executed by Herod Antipas, he is also attested by Josephus, who reports that many Jews saw Antipas's later military defeat as divine judgment for the killing.
people.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals §6043: born 5 BC, about six months before Jesus (Luke 1:26, 36). His ministry began in the fifteenth year of Tiberius (Luke 3:1; §6282-6283); imprisoned AD 30 after the first Passover (John 3:24; Mark 1:14; §6311) and beheaded AD 32 shortly before the feeding of the 5,000 (Matt 14:12-13; §6362). Josephus (Ant. 18.116-119) names Machaerus.

people.name: Lazarus
people.description: Brother of Mary and Martha; raised from the dead by Jesus after four days.
people.dateNotes: John 11:1-44; 12:1-11. Birth and death years are estimates. Later traditions of his life (bishop of Kition on Cyprus, or Marseille) are legendary; Scripture is silent.

people.name: Mary Magdalene
people.description: Follower of Jesus; first witness of the resurrection.
people.dateNotes: Luke 8:2; Mark 15:40; 16:9; John 20:1-18. Birth and death years are estimates. She is not the sister of Lazarus (that is Mary of Bethany), and the Gospels do not identify her with the sinful woman of Luke 7; that identification is a later Western tradition (Gregory the Great, AD 591). Traditions of her later life (Ephesus; Provence) are late.

people.name: Barabbas
people.description: Criminal released by Pilate instead of Jesus at the crowd's demand.
people.dateNotes: Matt 27:15-26. Released instead of Jesus in AD 33 (AD 30 on the alternative). No further record; birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Cleopas
people.description: Disciple who encountered the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.

people.name: Cornelius
people.description: Roman centurion in Caesarea; first Gentile convert. His household received the Holy Spirit.

people.name: Ethiopian Eunuch
people.description: Official of the Ethiopian queen Candace; baptized by Philip after reading Isaiah.

people.name: Ananias and Sapphira
people.description: Husband and wife who lied to the Holy Spirit about the price of their property; both struck dead.
people.dateNotes: Acts 5:1-11. Ussher, Annals §6514: AD 33, soon after Pentecost. Was 34. Birth year is an estimate. Death: Ussher, Annals 6514: AD 33, soon after Pentecost (Acts 5:1-11); earlier row had AD 34.

people.name: Eunice
people.description: Jewish believer of Lystra and mother of Timothy. Paul praises the "unfeigned faith" that dwelt first in Timothy's grandmother Lois and then in Eunice (2 Tim 1:5). Timothy's father was a Greek whom Scripture does not name (Acts 16:1).
people.dateNotes: Estimate only, about a generation before Timothy (born c. AD 17). Scripture gives no dates. 2 Tim 1:5 names Lois as Timothy's grandmother and Eunice as his mother; that Lois was Eunice's mother, not Timothy's paternal grandmother, is the natural reading but is not stated.

scripture.context: A Jewess who believed; her husband a Greek

people.name: Mary, mother of John Mark
people.description: Jerusalem believer in whose house many were praying when Peter came knocking after his release from prison (Acts 12:12). Her son was John, surnamed Mark. Colossians 4:10 calls Mark "sister's son to Barnabas" (KJV; the Greek anepsios is often rendered "cousin"), which makes her Barnabas's sister (or, if the word means cousin, his relative).
people.dateNotes: Estimate only, about a generation before Mark (born c. AD 15). The event is dated to AD 44 (Acts 12). Her husband is not named.

scripture.context: Peter comes to her house after his release
Mother of Mark, whom Barnabas is related to

people.name: Peter
people.description: A Galilean fisherman whom Jesus called to lead the apostles, remembered for his bold confession, his denial, and his restoration. He preached at Pentecost, opened the door to Gentile believers at Cornelius's house, and by early tradition was martyred in Rome under Nero. His wife is not named: the Gospels mention his mother-in-law (Mark 1:30) and Paul says Cephas took a wife with him on his travels (1 Cor 9:5).
people.dateNotes: Scripture does not record his death; Jesus foretells it (John 21:18-19). Ussher, Annals 6949, following early church tradition (Eusebius), dates the martyrdom of Peter and Paul at Rome to 29 June AD 67. Many modern scholars prefer about AD 64-68, under Nero.

events.role: Apostle who answered for the others

people.name: James, brother of Jesus
people.description: The Lord's brother who came to faith after the resurrection and became the acknowledged leader of the Jerusalem church, remembered as James the Just. Paul names him a pillar, the historian Josephus records his execution, and the practical wisdom of his letter still guides believers.
people.dateNotes: Acts 15:13-21; Gal 1:19; 2:9; James 1:1. Josephus (Ant. 20.200) records his stoning (Ussher: AD 63; commonly AD 62), between the death of Festus and the arrival of Albinus; Hegesippus (in Eusebius) gives a fuller account. Birth year is an estimate that assumes the brothers were younger sons of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view). The Orthodox tradition holds they were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (older than Jesus); the Catholic tradition, following Jerome, holds they were cousins. Death: Ussher, Annals 6885-6887: AD 63, after the death of Festus (Josephus Ant. 20.200); many modern scholars give AD 62.

people.name: Stephen
people.description: First Christian martyr.
people.dateNotes: Born c. AD 1 (estimated). A Hellenistic Jewish believer, mature enough to be chosen as one of the Seven (Acts 6:5). Stoned: Ussher, Annals §6519-6521, AD 33 (was c. AD 35; Paul's conversion follows in AD 35, §6533). Death: Ussher, Annals 6518-6521: stoned late AD 33 (Acts 7:58-60); earlier row had AD 35.

people.name: Joses, brother of Jesus
people.description: Brother of Jesus mentioned in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55.
people.dateNotes: Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55. Birth year is an estimate that assumes the brothers were younger sons of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view). The Orthodox tradition holds they were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (older than Jesus); the Catholic tradition, following Jerome, holds they were cousins.

scripture.context: Named among the brothers of Jesus

people.name: Andronicus
people.description: Jewish Christian in Rome whom Paul calls his kinsman and fellow prisoner, 'of note among the apostles' and in Christ before him. Usually paired with Junia.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. In Christ before Paul (converted about 35), so born by about the turn of the era; named in Romans (60).

people.name: Junia
people.description: Christian in Rome, greeted with Andronicus as Paul's kinsman and fellow prisoner, 'of note among the apostles'. Most ancient writers read the name as a woman's, and 'apostle' here may mean one sent out rather than one of the Twelve; readers differ on both points.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Same as Andronicus: in Christ before Paul, named in Romans (60).

people.name: Matthew
people.description: Tax collector called by Jesus (Matt 9:9), one of the Twelve; traditionally the author of the first Gospel. Mark 2:14 calls him Levi the son of Alpheus; whether this is the father of James son of Alphaeus is not stated.
people.dateNotes: Matt 9:9; 10:3; called Levi son of Alphaeus in Mark 2:14 and Levi in Luke 5:27. Birth and death years are estimates; Scripture does not record his death and later traditions of it disagree.

people.name: Simon, brother of Jesus
people.description: Brother of Jesus mentioned in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55. Not to be confused with Simon Peter or Simon the Zealot.
people.dateNotes: Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55. Birth year is an estimate that assumes the brothers were younger sons of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view). The Orthodox tradition holds they were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (older than Jesus); the Catholic tradition, following Jerome, holds they were cousins.

scripture.context: Named among the brothers of Jesus

people.name: James, son of Zebedee
people.description: Son of Zebedee and brother of John, one of the inner three with Peter and John. Herod Agrippa I had him killed with the sword (Acts 12:2), the only one of the Twelve whose martyrdom Scripture records. Matthew 27:56 mentions "the mother of Zebedee's children" at the cross; Mark 15:40 names Salome in the same group, and she is commonly identified with her (an inference).
people.dateNotes: Killed shortly before Peter's arrest at Passover (Acts 12:1-3); Agrippa died soon after in AD 44 (Acts 12:23; Josephus Ant. 19.343-352), so AD 44. Birth year is an estimate. The tradition of his preaching in Spain and burial at Santiago de Compostela is medieval.

people.name: Judas Iscariot
people.description: Apostle who betrayed Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
people.dateNotes: Matthew 26:14-16, 47-50; 27:3-10; Acts 1:16-20. Death in the passion week: Ussher, Annals §6473 (AD 33). Birth is an estimate.

people.name: Jude, brother of Jesus
people.description: Brother of Jesus mentioned in Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55. Traditionally identified as the author of the Epistle of Jude.
people.dateNotes: Mark 6:3 (Juda); Matthew 13:55 (Judas); Jude 1:1 ('brother of James'). Birth year is an estimate that assumes the brothers were younger sons of Mary and Joseph (the common Protestant view). The Orthodox tradition holds they were sons of Joseph by an earlier marriage (older than Jesus); the Catholic tradition, following Jerome, holds they were cousins.

scripture.context: Named among the brothers of Jesus

people.name: Paul
people.description: A Pharisee who persecuted the church until an encounter with the risen Jesus made him the apostle to the Gentiles. His missionary journeys and letters shaped Christian theology more than any other early figure, and the Gallio inscription at Delphi helps anchor his career in history.
people.dateNotes: Scripture does not record his death; he expects it in 2 Tim 4:6-8. Ussher, Annals 6949, following early church tradition (Eusebius), dates the martyrdom of Peter and Paul at Rome to 29 June AD 67. His journeys and imprisonments follow Acts and Ussher: conversion AD 35, the council AD 52 (Gal 2:1), Rome AD 63-65 (Acts 28:30). Many modern scholars prefer about AD 64-68 for his death.

events.role: Carried the relief to Jerusalem (as Saul)

people.name: Barnabas
people.description: Companion of Paul on first missionary journey. Colossians 4:10 calls Mark his sister's son (in other versions, cousin).
people.dateNotes: Joses surnamed Barnabas, a Levite of Cyprus (Acts 4:36). Birth year is an estimate. A 5th-century tradition (Acts of Barnabas) has him martyred at Salamis on Cyprus, c. AD 61; Acts is silent.

people.name: Andrew
people.description: Brother of Peter; one of the first disciples called. Peter and Andrew were sons of Jona (John 1:42; Matt 16:17).
people.dateNotes: John 1:35-42; Matt 4:18-20. Death c. AD 65 by crucifixion at Patras in Achaea is later tradition (Acts of Andrew); the X-shaped cross is a medieval detail. Scripture is silent.

events.role: Pointed out the boy with loaves and fish (John 6:8)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table

people.name: Philip the Apostle
people.description: Apostle from Bethsaida who brought Nathanael to Jesus.
people.dateNotes: John 1:43-48; 6:5-7; 14:8-9. Death c. AD 80 at Hierapolis is tradition, and ancient writers sometimes confused him with Philip the Evangelist. Scripture is silent.

events.role: Asked by Jesus where to buy bread (John 6:5-7)
Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table; asked to see the Father (John 14:8)

people.name: Bartholomew
people.description: Apostle whom Jesus described as an Israelite without guile.
people.dateNotes: Matt 10:3; John 1:45-51. Traditionally identified with Nathanael of Cana (John 21:2). Death c. AD 70 in Armenia is later tradition; Scripture is silent.

events.role: Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table

scripture.context: Tradition identifies Bartholomew with Nathanael; John does not name him as such
Named in the lists of the Twelve (also Mark 3:18; Luke 6:14; Acts 1:13)

people.name: Thomas
people.description: Apostle known for his doubt and powerful confession of faith.
people.dateNotes: John 11:16; 14:5; 20:24-29. Death c. AD 72 at Mylapore near Chennai, India, is tradition (Acts of Thomas; the St Thomas Christians); Scripture is silent.

people.name: James, son of Alphaeus
people.description: One of the twelve apostles; sometimes called James the Less. Matthew 10:3 names his father as Alphaeus; Matthew (Levi) also has a father Alphaeus (Mark 2:14), but the text does not say they are brothers.
people.dateNotes: Matt 10:3; Mark 3:18. Birth and death years are estimates. Later traditions of his death vary, and the year 62 may be borrowed from James the brother of Jesus. His identification with 'James the less' (Mark 15:40) is traditional but uncertain. Scripture records nothing further.

events.role: Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table

people.name: Thaddaeus
people.description: Apostle also known as Judas son of James; asked Jesus a question at the Last Supper.
people.dateNotes: Matt 10:3; Luke 6:16; John 14:22; Acts 1:13. Luke calls him 'Judas of James' (KJV 'brother of James'). Not Judas Iscariot, and traditionally distinguished from Jude the brother of Jesus. Death c. AD 65 is later tradition (Armenian and Syriac); Scripture is silent.

events.role: Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table

scripture.context: Thaddaeus is named in the lists of the Twelve
Judas (not Iscariot), identified with Thaddaeus by inference
Luke lists Judas son of James in this place, commonly identified with Thaddaeus

people.name: Simon the Zealot
people.description: Apostle who may have been a member of the Zealot movement.
people.dateNotes: Matt 10:4; Luke 6:15; Acts 1:13. 'Zealot' may describe his zeal or the Zealot movement. Death c. AD 65 is later tradition with conflicting accounts; Scripture is silent.

events.role: Among the apostles gathered in Jerusalem (Acts 1:13; 2:1)
One of the eleven sent out (Matt 28:16-20)
One of the twelve at the table

people.name: Matthias
people.description: Chosen by lot to replace Judas Iscariot among the twelve.
people.dateNotes: Acts 1:21-26. Later tradition places his ministry in Judea, Cappadocia or Ethiopia; Scripture does not mention him after Acts 1. Birth and death years are estimates.

people.name: Silas
people.description: Prominent member of the Jerusalem church; companion of Paul on the second missionary journey.
people.dateNotes: Acts 15:22-40; 16-17; 1 Thessalonians 1:1.

people.name: Ananias of Damascus
people.description: Disciple in Damascus who baptized Paul after his conversion on the road to Damascus.

people.name: Agabus
people.description: Christian prophet who predicted a famine and later warned Paul of his arrest in Jerusalem.

events.role: Prophet who came to Antioch and foretold the famine (Acts 11:27-28)

people.name: Dorcas
people.description: Disciple in Joppa known for charitable works; raised from the dead by Peter.

people.name: Philip the Evangelist
people.description: One of the Seven; evangelized Samaria and baptized the Ethiopian eunuch on the Gaza road. Luke says he had four unmarried daughters who prophesied (Acts 21:9); they are not named.
people.dateNotes: Acts 6:5; 8:4-40; 21:8-9. Death c. AD 70 is an estimate; the Hierapolis tradition is sometimes confused with Philip the Apostle. Scripture is silent.

people.name: John the Apostle
people.description: A son of Zebedee and member of Jesus' inner circle, traditionally identified as the beloved disciple behind the fourth Gospel. Linked with Ephesus and exile on Patmos, his legacy endures in the earliest known New Testament fragment, a papyrus scrap of his Gospel known as P52. Matthew 27:56 mentions "the mother of Zebedee's children" at the cross; Mark 15:40 names Salome in the same group, and she is commonly identified with her (an inference).
people.dateNotes: His death c. AD 98-100 at Ephesus is early church tradition (Irenaeus AH 2.22.5; Eusebius HE 3.23); Scripture is silent. His identification with the beloved disciple and with the author of the Gospel, the letters and Revelation is traditional and debated; John 21:20-24 does not name him.

people.name: Vespasian
people.description: Roman general sent to put down the Jewish revolt in AD 66. He was proclaimed emperor in AD 69 and left the siege of Jerusalem to his son Titus. He ruled until AD 79.
people.dateNotes: Standard Roman chronology: born 17 November AD 9, emperor 69-79, died 23 June AD 79.

events.role: Emperor who sent his son to finish the war

people.name: Luke
people.description: Physician; author of Luke and Acts.
people.dateNotes: Born c. AD 10 (estimate); from Antioch according to Eusebius (HE 3.4). Physician (Col 4:14); traditionally the author of Luke-Acts. The Anti-Marcionite Prologue says he died in Boeotia aged 84, which with the birth estimate gives c. AD 94.

people.name: Titus
people.description: Gentile convert and co-worker of Paul; led the church in Crete.
people.dateNotes: Galatians 2:1-3; 2 Corinthians 7-8; Titus 1:4-5.

events.role: Went up to Jerusalem with Paul and Barnabas; not compelled to be circumcised (Gal 2:1-3)

people.name: Priscilla
people.description: Wife of Aquila; together they mentored Apollos and hosted house churches.

people.name: Aquila
people.description: Husband of Priscilla; tentmaker who worked with Paul in Corinth.

people.name: Apollos
people.description: Eloquent Alexandrian Jew who preached powerfully but was further taught by Priscilla and Aquila.
people.dateNotes: Acts 18:24-28; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4-6.

events.role: Named in the letter; Paul urged him to visit Corinth (1 Cor 16:12)

people.name: Philemon
people.description: Wealthy Christian in Colossae to whom Paul wrote about the slave Onesimus.
people.dateNotes: Philemon 1-25.

people.name: Lydia
people.description: Seller of purple cloth in Philippi; first European convert. Hosted Paul and Silas.

people.name: Festus
people.description: Roman governor who succeeded Felix; before whom Paul appealed to Caesar.
people.dateNotes: Acts 25:1-12; 26:24-32. Procurator AD 62-63 on Ussher (commonly c. AD 60-62; some date his arrival to 59); died in office (Josephus Ant. 20.197, 200). Birth year is an estimate. Ussher, Annals 6868, 6885: arrived as governor AD 62 and died in office AD 63 (Josephus Ant. 20.197).

people.name: Epaphras
people.description: Founder or teacher of the church at Colossae, who brought Paul news of it in prison and prayed hard for it and for Laodicea and Hierapolis. Paul calls him a fellow servant and fellow prisoner. He may be the same person as Epaphroditus, but the text does not say so; this timeline keeps them apart.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in the prison letters (about 64); birth set about 10.

scripture.context: Prays and labours for the churches of the Lycus valley

people.name: Onesiphorus
people.description: Christian of Ephesus whose household Paul blesses. He often refreshed Paul and was not ashamed of his chain, and in Rome he searched hard until he found him.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in 2 Timothy (about 66); birth set about 10. Paul wishes mercy on his 'house' and greets it (2 Tim 4:19), which some readers take to mean he had died; the text does not say.

scripture.context: Refreshes Paul and finds him in Rome

people.name: Archippus
people.description: Fellow soldier of Paul addressed in Philemon, who is told in Colossians to take heed to the ministry he received in the Lord. He seems to have belonged to Philemon's household church.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in Colossians and Philemon (about 64); birth set about 10.

people.name: Stephanas
people.description: Corinthian whose household Paul baptised and called the firstfruits of Achaia. He gave himself to serving the saints, and with Fortunatus and Achaicus visited Paul and brought him news from Corinth.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Baptised by Paul during the 18 months at Corinth (about 54-55); visits Paul around the time 1 Corinthians was written (59); birth set about 10.

people.name: Salome daughter of Herodias
people.description: Daughter of Herodias who danced before Herod and requested John the Baptist's head. Married Philip the tetrarch, according to Josephus.
people.dateNotes: Estimate: she was a girl when she danced before Herod Antipas, about AD 31-32 (Mark 6:22). Her name comes from Josephus (Antiquities 18.5.4); the Gospels do not name her.

people.name: Mark
people.description: Companion of Paul and Barnabas (Acts 12:25; 15:37-39) and later of Peter (1 Pet 5:13); traditionally the author of the second Gospel. His mother was Mary of Jerusalem, whose house served as a meeting place (Acts 12:12). Colossians 4:10 calls him "sister's son to Barnabas" (often translated cousin).
people.dateNotes: Acts 12:12, 25; 15:37-39; Col 4:10; 2 Tim 4:11; 1 Pet 5:13. His identification with the evangelist and with the Mark of 1 Peter is traditional. Death c. AD 68 at Alexandria is later tradition (Eusebius HE 2.16 records his Alexandrian mission).

scripture.context: Son of Mary, in whose house the church prayed

people.name: Rhoda
people.description: Servant girl who answered the door when Peter was freed from prison; was so overjoyed she forgot to open it.

people.name: Aristarchus
people.description: Macedonian of Thessalonica and companion of Paul. He was seized in the Ephesus riot, travelled with Paul toward Asia, sailed with him on the voyage to Rome, and is called Paul's fellow prisoner and fellow labourer.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Appears in Acts 19-27 (about 57-62) and in the prison letters (about 64); birth set about 15.

people.name: Epaphroditus
people.description: Messenger of the Philippian church who brought Paul their gift in prison. He fell nearly fatally ill, recovered, and was sent back with Paul's letter to Philippi.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in Philippians (about 64); birth set about 15. Not the same person as Epaphras of Colossae as far as the text shows.

scripture.context: Sent with the letter after near-fatal illness

people.name: Erastus
people.description: Helper of Paul whom he sent with Timothy from Ephesus into Macedonia. A man named Erastus, the city treasurer, sends greetings in Romans from Corinth, and 2 Timothy says Erastus stayed at Corinth. The text does not say that all three are one man, though many readers think so.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Acts 19:22 (about 57), Romans (60) and 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 15.

people.name: Gaius of Macedonia
people.description: Companion of Paul from Macedonia who was seized with Aristarchus by the Ephesus mob. The text calls him a Macedonian; the Gaius of Derbe in Acts 20:4 is described differently, so this timeline treats them as separate men, though some readers identify them.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Acts 19:29 (about 57); birth set about 15.

people.name: Gaius of Derbe
people.description: Man of Derbe in Lycaonia who accompanied Paul into Asia at the end of the third journey, among a party that included Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Acts 20:4 (about 56); birth set about 15. Some manuscripts read 'Doberius' for 'Derbe', and some readers equate him with the Macedonian Gaius of Acts 19:29.

people.name: Gaius of Corinth
people.description: Corinthian baptised by Paul and later host to Paul and to the whole church there, who sends greetings in Romans. He is probably the Gaius of 1 Corinthians 1:14.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Baptised during the Corinth ministry (about 54-55) and sending greetings from Corinth when Romans was written (60); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Host of Paul and the whole church

people.name: Tryphena
people.description: Woman greeted by Paul in Rome as one who labours in the Lord. KJV spells the name Tryphaena. Often thought to be a sister or relative of Tryphosa, though the text does not say.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in Romans (60); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Greeted as a labourer in the Lord

people.name: Tryphosa
people.description: Woman greeted by Paul in Rome as one who labours in the Lord, named together with Tryphena.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in Romans (60); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Greeted as a labourer in the Lord

people.name: Euodia
people.description: Woman of the Philippian church who laboured with Paul in the gospel. Paul urges her and Syntyche to be of one mind in the Lord. KJV spells the name Euodias.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Philippians (about 64); birth set about 15.

events.role: urged to be of one mind

people.name: Syntyche
people.description: Woman of the Philippian church who laboured with Paul in the gospel. Paul urges her and Euodia to be of one mind in the Lord.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Philippians (about 64); birth set about 15.

events.role: urged to be of one mind

people.name: Hymenaeus
people.description: False teacher whom Paul says he handed over to Satan so that he would learn not to blaspheme, and who with Philetus taught that the resurrection had already happened. KJV spells the name Hymeneus.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in 1 Timothy (65) and 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Teaches that the resurrection is past

people.name: Philetus
people.description: False teacher named with Hymenaeus, whose talk spread like gangrene and who overturned the faith of some by saying the resurrection was already past.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Teaches that the resurrection is past

people.name: Alexander the coppersmith
people.description: Man who did Paul much harm and strongly opposed his message, so that Paul warns Timothy about him. He may be the Alexander whom Paul handed over to Satan in 1 Timothy 1:20, but the text does not say; he is also not clearly the Alexander of the Ephesus riot (Acts 19:33).
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 15.

scripture.context: Possibly the Alexander delivered to Satan

people.name: Tertius
people.description: Christian who wrote down Paul's letter to the Romans as Paul dictated it, and who adds his own greeting in the Lord.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Romans (60); birth set about 15.

people.name: Timothy
people.description: Paul's protégé; recipient of two epistles. His mother Eunice and grandmother Lois were believers (2 Tim 1:5); his father was a Greek whom Scripture does not name (Acts 16:1).
people.dateNotes: Born at Lystra to a Jewish mother (Eunice) and a Greek father (Acts 16:1; 2 Tim 1:5); still young when Paul wrote 1 Timothy (1 Tim 4:12). Birth c. AD 17 is an estimate. Later tradition (Acts of Timothy) has him killed at Ephesus c. AD 97.

scripture.context: Son of a Jewish believer and a Greek father

people.name: Phoebe
people.description: Deaconess of the church at Cenchreae; commended by Paul as a patron and letter-carrier of Romans.

people.name: Tychicus
people.description: Christian from the province of Asia who travelled with Paul and carried his letters to Ephesus and Colossae, telling the churches how Paul was faring. Paul later sent him to Ephesus and offered to send him to Titus on Crete.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Active from Paul's third journey (Acts 20:4, about 56) through 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 20 so he is an adult in 56.

scripture.context: Carries the letter and news to Ephesus
Carries the letter and news to Colossae

people.name: Trophimus
people.description: Gentile Christian of Ephesus who travelled with Paul. Jews in Jerusalem falsely supposed Paul had brought him into the temple, which sparked Paul's arrest. Paul later left him sick at Miletus.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in Acts 20-21 (about 56-60) and 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 20.

events.role: seen with Paul in the city

scripture.context: Seen with Paul in Jerusalem; cause of the riot

people.name: Demas
people.description: Co-worker of Paul during his Roman imprisonment, who sent greetings with Luke. Near the end of Paul's life he left him, having loved the present world, and went to Thessalonica.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Named in the prison letters (about 64) and 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 20.

people.name: Zenas the lawyer
people.description: Lawyer whom Paul asks Titus to help on his journey together with Apollos, so that they lack nothing. It is not clear whether he was a Roman or a Jewish legal expert.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Titus (65); birth set about 20.

scripture.context: Sent on his way with Apollos

people.name: Artemas
people.description: Co-worker of Paul whom he planned to send to Titus on Crete, or else Tychicus, so that Titus could come to meet him at Nicopolis.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. Titus (65); birth set about 20.

people.name: Linus
people.description: Christian in Rome who sends greetings to Timothy in Paul's last letter. Early church writers (Irenaeus, Eusebius) name a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles and identify him with this man; that identification is tradition, not stated in Scripture.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 20. Tradition's later dates for his bishopric are not used here.

people.name: Carpus
people.description: Christian of Troas with whom Paul left his cloak, books and parchments, and whom Paul asks Timothy to visit on his way to Rome.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. 2 Timothy (66); birth set about 20.

scripture.context: Keeps Paul's cloak and books at Troas

people.name: Herod Agrippa II
people.description: Last of the Herodian line; heard Paul's defense at Caesarea. Said Paul almost persuaded him to be a Christian. Sisters of Agrippa II: Bernice (Acts 25:13) and Drusilla (Acts 24:24).
people.dateNotes: Acts 25:13-26:32. Born AD 27 or 28 (Josephus Ant. 19.354); king of Chalcis from AD 50, later of territories to the north-east; died c. AD 92-100 (Photius gives AD 100).

people.name: Bernice
people.description: Daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Drusilla. She came with Agrippa II to Caesarea to greet Festus and heard Paul's defense with him (Acts 25:13; 26:30).
people.dateNotes: Josephus (Ant. 19.276-277): born c. AD 28. The year of her death is not recorded; she was still living in the 70s, when she was with Titus in Rome.

scripture.context: Comes with Agrippa II to greet Festus

people.name: Onesimus
people.description: Runaway slave of Philemon whom Paul sent back with a letter asking Philemon to receive him no longer as a slave but as a beloved brother (Philem 16).
people.dateNotes: Philem 1:10-21; Col 4:9.

events.role: Runaway slave Paul sends back with the letter

people.name: Gaius, addressee of 3 John
people.description: Beloved friend of the elder John, praised for walking in the truth and for hospitality to travelling brothers. He is the one to whom 3 John is addressed. The text does not say whether he is one of the other Gaiuses named in the New Testament.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. 3 John (about 90); birth set about 30 so he is an adult in 90.

people.name: Diotrephes
people.description: Church leader who loved to have the first place, rejected the elder's authority and messengers, spoke against him with malicious words, and put out of the church those who would welcome the brothers. John says he will deal with him when he comes.
people.dateNotes: Estimate; Scripture gives no birth or death year. 3 John (about 90); birth set about 30.

scripture.context: Refuses the elder and expels the brothers

people.name: Ignatius of Antioch
people.description: Bishop of Antioch and early Church Father. His seven letters on church order, the Eucharist, and martyrdom are among the earliest post-apostolic writings.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is unknown; c. 35 is a conventional estimate. Martyred in Rome under Trajan (reigned 98-117), traditionally dated c. 108; some scholars place it as late as c. 110-117.

people.name: Nero
people.description: Fifth Roman emperor (AD 54-68). He was the Caesar to whom Paul appealed (Acts 25:11). Tacitus records that he blamed the Christians for the great fire of AD 64 and put many to death; church tradition places the deaths of Peter and Paul in his reign. Born Lucius Domitius Ahenobarbus, he was Claudius's stepson and was adopted by him in AD 50, after which he succeeded him.
people.dateNotes: Born 15 December AD 37; died 9 June AD 68. Acts 25:11; Tacitus, Annals 15.44.

people.name: Drusilla
people.description: Youngest daughter of Herod Agrippa I and wife of the Roman governor Felix. She was a Jewess, and with Felix she heard Paul speak about the faith in Christ (Acts 24:24).
people.dateNotes: Ussher, Annals 6592: born AD 38 (aged six at her father Agrippa I's death in AD 44; Josephus Ant. 19.354). She married Felix c. AD 54 (6795; Josephus Ant. 20.141-143 puts it about AD 53) and heard Paul with him in AD 60 (Acts 24:24). Death not recorded.

scripture.context: Comes with her husband Felix to hear Paul

people.name: Titus, Roman emperor
people.description: Son of Vespasian who commanded the Roman army at the siege of Jerusalem, ending with the burning of the Temple in AD 70. He became emperor in AD 79 and died after two years. Not to be confused with Titus, the companion of Paul.
people.dateNotes: Standard Roman chronology: born 30 December AD 39, emperor 79-81, died 13 September AD 81.

people.name: Polycarp of Smyrna
people.description: Bishop of Smyrna, a leading figure of the generation after the apostles who, according to Irenaeus, had known the Apostle John. At his martyrdom he declared "Eighty-six years I have served Him, and He never did me any injury."
people.dateNotes: Birth c. 69 is inferred from his '86 years' remark (which could mean his age or the years since his conversion) and is uncertain. Martyred on 22/23 February in 155 or 156, the standard modern dating; Eusebius's Chronicle points to c. 166-167, which most scholars now reject.

people.name: Irenaeus of Lyon
people.description: Bishop of Lyon who, by his own account, heard Polycarp as a young man. His work Against Heresies is foundational for early Christian orthodoxy and appeals to Scripture, the rule of faith and the succession of bishops from the apostles as tests of true teaching.
people.dateNotes: Born in Asia Minor (probably Smyrna) c. 130-142; died c. 202. Both dates are estimates.

people.name: Tertullian
people.description: Early Latin Christian writer in Carthage. The earliest surviving Latin use of the word trinitas is his, and he shaped much of Latin theological vocabulary. Later he joined the Montanist movement, which is why he is not always counted among the Church Fathers.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 155 in Carthage; died c. 220. Both dates are estimates.

people.name: Origen of Alexandria
people.description: Prolific scholar and head of the catechetical school in Alexandria, later teaching at Caesarea in Palestine. Pioneered textual criticism and allegorical interpretation of Scripture. His Hexapla set the Hebrew Old Testament beside several Greek versions in parallel columns. Some of his speculative teachings were later condemned, but his influence on Eastern and Western exegesis was immense.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 185 in Alexandria; died c. 253-254 in Tyre, after suffering torture in the Decian persecution (250-251).

people.name: Diocletian
people.description: Roman emperor from 284 to 305 who reorganised the empire under a shared rule of four. In 303 he and his colleagues began the last and most severe empire-wide persecution of Christians. He abdicated in 305.
people.dateNotes: Born about 244; abdicated 305; died c. 311 (3 December 311 is usual; some give 312). The first persecution edict was issued at Nicomedia in February 303.

people.name: Constantius I Chlorus
people.description: Roman emperor in the West (Caesar from 293, Augustus 305-306), father of Constantine the Great. His eastern colleagues carried out the Great Persecution, but his own rule in Gaul and Britain was mild. He died at York, where his troops proclaimed Constantine.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 250; died 25 July 306 at Eboracum (York).

events.role: Dying emperor; his death opens the succession

people.name: Helena, mother of Constantine
people.description: Mother of Constantine the Great, given the title Augusta by her son. Eusebius reports her pilgrimage to the Holy Land in her old age, and later tradition credits her with finding the True Cross. She is honored as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches. Whether she was Constantius's wife or concubine is debated.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 250 (from Eusebius, who says she was about 80 on her pilgrimage c. 327-328); died c. 330. Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.42-47. The finding of the Cross is a later tradition.

people.name: Tiridates III of Armenia
people.description: King of Armenia who, according to Armenian tradition, was converted by Gregory the Illuminator and made Armenia the first state to adopt Christianity as its official religion.
people.dateNotes: His reign is usually given as about 287-330; birth year is an estimate. The date of his conversion is traditionally 301 and debated.

people.name: Gregory the Illuminator
people.description: Traditional founder and first head of the Armenian Church. According to Armenian tradition he converted King Tiridates III, who made Christianity the state religion of Armenia.
people.dateNotes: Dates are traditional and approximate; the Armenian sources are later accounts. The conversion is traditionally put at 301, though some scholars date it a decade or so later.

events.role: Baptised the king and led the church

people.name: Galerius
people.description: Roman emperor who is generally thought to have urged Diocletian toward persecuting Christians. In 311, shortly before his death, he issued an edict of toleration ending the persecution in the East.
people.dateNotes: Born about 260; died in 311, soon after the Edict of Serdica (also called the Edict of Toleration).

people.name: Constantine the Great
people.description: Roman emperor who, after the Milvian Bridge (312), favored Christianity, agreed with Licinius to extend toleration (313), and convened the Council of Nicaea (325). He was baptized shortly before his death in 337. Christianity became legal and favored, not the state religion, under him. His mother was Helena and his father Constantius Chlorus.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 272 (Naissus); died 22 May 337 near Nicomedia.

events.role: Imperial sponsor of the building programme

people.name: Athanasius of Alexandria
people.description: Bishop of Alexandria who defended Christ's full deity against Arianism through five exiles, holding the line for the Nicene faith. His Easter festal letter contains the earliest known list of exactly the twenty-seven New Testament books, a landmark in the history of the canon.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 296 (estimates c. 293-298); died 2 May 373. Exiled five times by common count.

people.name: Patricius, father of Augustine
people.description: Pagan town councillor of Thagaste, Augustine's father, who was baptized shortly before his death. He is known from Augustine's Confessions (book 2 and book 9), which describes his ambitions for his son's education.
people.dateNotes: Estimate. Augustine says he died when Augustine was seventeen, c. 371 (Confessions 3.4). His birth year is inferred.

people.name: Gregory of Nazianzus
people.description: Cappadocian bishop and theologian, honoured in the Eastern Church as "the Theologian." He led the Nicene congregation in Constantinople and briefly presided over the Council of 381 before resigning.
people.dateNotes: Born about 329-330; died 390.

events.role: Bishop who led the council at first

people.name: Monica of Hippo
people.description: Christian mother of Augustine of Hippo, who prayed and wept for his conversion for many years and followed him to Milan. She died at Ostia in 387 on the journey home to Africa, shortly after the conversation with her son recorded in the Confessions (book 9). Honored as a saint in the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
people.dateNotes: Born 331 in Thagaste; died 387 at Ostia. Augustine, Confessions 9.8-13.

people.name: Gregory of Nyssa
people.description: Cappadocian bishop and theologian, younger brother of Basil the Great. He took an important part in the Council of Constantinople in 381 and in shaping the doctrine of the Trinity.
people.dateNotes: Birth about 335; death about 395 (last attested that year).

people.name: Ambrose of Milan
people.description: Roman governor made Bishop of Milan by popular acclaim in 374. His preaching influenced Augustine of Hippo, and he baptised him at Easter 387. Western tradition counts him one of the four Doctors of the Church.
people.dateNotes: Born about 339; died 4 April 397.

people.name: Jerome
people.description: A learned and irascible monk and biblical scholar who revised the Latin Gospels and Psalms and translated most of the Old Testament into Latin from the Hebrew, settling in Bethlehem around 386. The resulting Vulgate, a composite text that gradually replaced the Old Latin versions, became the Bible of the Western church for about a thousand years.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 347 (some scholars c. 342) in Stridon; died 30 September 420 in Bethlehem.

people.name: John Chrysostom
people.description: Archbishop of Constantinople, famed for his preaching and his expositions of Scripture, who criticized the wealthy and the imperial court and died in exile. Honored in the Eastern and Western churches; his name means Golden-mouthed.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 347 (344-354) in Antioch; died 14 September 407 at Comana in Pontus.

people.name: Theodosius I
people.description: Roman emperor who, in 380, made Nicene Christianity the religion of the empire. He summoned the Council of Constantinople in 381, which confirmed the Nicene faith.
people.dateNotes: Born 11 January 347, emperor in the East 379 and of the whole empire 392-395, died 17 January 395.

people.name: Augustine of Hippo
people.description: A North African rhetorician converted in a Milan garden who became bishop of Hippo and the most influential theologian of the Western church. His Confessions pioneered spiritual autobiography, and his teaching on grace, sin, and the City of God shaped Catholic and Protestant thought alike. His mother Monica and father Patricius are known from the Confessions; his son Adeodatus was born in 372.
people.dateNotes: Born November 13, 354 in Thagaste; died August 28, 430 in Hippo.

people.name: Adeodatus
people.description: Son of Augustine and his unnamed concubine. He was baptized with his father at Milan in 387 and appears as a speaker in Augustine's dialogue De Magistro. He died young, not long after returning to Africa.
people.dateNotes: Born 372 in Carthage; died c. 390. Confessions 4.2, 9.6. Augustine's companion is not named in any source.

people.name: Cyril of Alexandria
people.description: Patriarch of Alexandria from 412 to 444. He opposed Nestorius and presided over the Council of Ephesus in 431, which affirmed the title Theotokos ("God-bearer") for Mary.
people.dateNotes: Born about 376; died 27 June 444.

people.name: Patrick of Ireland
people.description: Missionary to Ireland. Captured as a slave at about 16, he escaped and later returned to evangelize the Irish. Irish Christianity went on to become a notable center of monastic learning and mission.
people.dateNotes: Traditional dates c. 385-461; many modern scholars place his mission in the later fifth century (died c. 490s). Born in Roman Britain; his own Confessio gives no years.

people.name: Nestorius
people.description: Patriarch of Constantinople from 428 who objected to calling Mary Theotokos. The Council of Ephesus deposed him in 431 and he died in exile in Egypt. The Church of the East, often called Nestorian, did not accept his condemnation as fair, and scholars still debate what he actually taught.
people.dateNotes: Born about 386; died after 451, probably that year. Exact dates are not recorded.

people.name: Marcian
people.description: Eastern Roman emperor from 450 to 457. He summoned the Council of Chalcedon in 451, together with his wife Pulcheria, to settle the disputes over the nature of Christ.
people.dateNotes: Born about 392; emperor 450-457; died January 457.

people.name: Pope Leo I
people.description: Bishop of Rome from 440 to 461. His letter to Flavian, known as the Tome of Leo, set out the teaching of two natures in one person of Christ and shaped the definition of Chalcedon in 451. He is also remembered for persuading Attila to withdraw from Italy in 452.
people.dateNotes: Birth year about 400; died 10 November 461.

events.role: Pope whose Tome shaped the definition

people.name: Theodosius II
people.description: Eastern Roman emperor from 408 to 450. He summoned the Council of Ephesus in 431 and the second Council of Ephesus in 449.
people.dateNotes: Born 10 April 401; died 28 July 450 after a riding accident.

people.name: Odoacer
people.description: Germanic military commander who deposed the last Western Roman emperor in 476 and ruled Italy as king. He was killed by Theodoric the Ostrogoth in 493.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is an estimate. He was killed 15 March 493.

people.name: Romulus Augustulus
people.description: The last emperor of the Western Roman Empire. A boy raised to the throne by his father in 475, he was deposed by Odoacer in 476. He was allowed to live, and little more is known of him.
people.dateNotes: Birth year is an estimate (a young teenager in 475-476). Deposed in September 476; the date of his death is unknown.

people.name: Benedict of Nursia
people.description: Founder of Monte Cassino and author of the Rule of St. Benedict, which became the standard rule of Western monasticism. Its balance of prayer, work and study, later summed up in the motto "ora et labora", shaped monastic communities that preserved learning in the early Middle Ages.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 480 in Nursia; died c. 547 (some sources c. 543) at Monte Cassino. Almost all details come from Gregory the Great's Dialogues, book II.

people.name: Gregory the Great
people.description: Pope from 590 to 604, who strengthened the Roman see, sent Augustine of Canterbury to England, and wrote the Pastoral Rule and the Dialogues (the main source for the life of Benedict). He is honored by Catholic and Orthodox churches.
people.dateNotes: Born c. 540 in Rome; died 12 March 604.

people.name: Aethelberht of Kent
people.description: King of Kent who received Augustine of Canterbury in 597 and was later baptised, the first Anglo-Saxon king to become Christian. His wife Bertha, a Frankish Christian, had already encouraged the faith at his court.
people.dateNotes: Born about 560; reigned about 590-616; baptism usually put about 601.

people.name: Muhammad
people.description: Arab religious and political leader of Mecca and Medina, regarded by Muslims as the final prophet and the one through whom the Quran was revealed. He founded the Muslim community; within a few years of his death in 632 the armies of his successors, the caliphs, began the conquests of the Byzantine and Persian territories.
